claims.text: Strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys are governed by the interaction between lattice distortion and dislocation mobility.
Increasing lattice distortion reduces dislocation mobility.
Increasing lattice distortion enhances alloy strength.
Atomic size mismatch among alloying elements can be systematically altered to vary lattice distortion.
Grain size and processing conditions can be held constant while atomic size mismatch is varied.
Lattice distortion magnitude can be quantified using atomic size mismatch and local strain fields.
Lattice distortion creates local strain fields.
Local strain fields impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases resistance to plastic deformation.
Increased resistance to plastic deformation enhances strength.
Alloys with greater lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than alloys with lower lattice distortion under identical testing conditions.
Alloys with greater lattice distortion will have lower ductility than alloys with lower lattice distortion under identical testing conditions.
Near-equiatomic alloys made from elements with similar atomic sizes provide a minimal-lattice-distortion baseline.
The proposed relationship applies under room-temperature, quasi-static loading.
The proposed relationship applies to FCC and BCC multi-component concentrated alloys that do not undergo phase separation or significant precipitation.
Short-range order and electronic effects may also influence the extent to which lattice distortion governs strength and deformation.
Tensile testing and TEM can be used to compare yield strength, elongation to failure, dislocation density, and dislocation mobility across the alloy series.
